title: The Ferry in the Mud

pages.text:
*The Bearer's Almanac, Entry 3: Water is lazy. It takes the lowest road and calls it wisdom.*

The ferry lay on its side, a flat sliver of wood wedged into the sucking mud of the dry channel bed. It was not broken. Merely trapped. It rested on a bar of packed silt that had once been a deep, dark lane of water. Auntie Mo stood over it, her bamboo pole tapping the ground with a rhythmic, impatient click. She was explaining to Wen the simple, brutal arithmetic of buoyancy.

"You see this line?" Mo said, pointing to a series of notches carved into the stern post of the boat. "They are called hands. One hand is a span, a palm’s width. When the river is full, the water sits at the fifth hand. Today, we are sitting at the bottom. Zero hands. And zero hands means the boat is dead."

Wen crouched, the mud cool and gritty against her knees. She touched the wood. It was smooth, oiled by decades of river traffic, but stiff with dried silt. "If I lift the water under it," Wen offered, her voice quiet, testing the idea, "it will float."

Mo looked down at her, her eyes sharp and unimpressed. "You lift the water, the water comes from somewhere else. You take it from the pool, the pool dries. You take it from the air, it freezes. Arithmetic, child. A boat is heavy. It is wood, iron, and the burden of every thing it has ever carried. You do not lift a boat by pulling the water. You pull the boat by moving the earth."

She picked up a short, curved spade from the sand. The blade was dull, the handle worn to a pale, smooth oval. "We do not summon the river," Mo said, her voice flat and final. "We invite it. And rivers are lazy. They take the lowest road. Our job is to make sure the lowest road goes where we want it to go."

Wen watched the spade bite into the mud. It was a small, honest motion. No magic. No sparks. No trembling air. Just dirt moving from one place to another. For the first time since the pool had dried, the world felt manageable. A problem with a solution that fit in her hands.
pages.image: Wen crouching beside a flat wooden ferry stuck on a mudbar, touching a notched stern post, Auntie Mo standing with a spade, dry river channel, morning light, dust motes.

pages.text:
They had been walking for an hour, the path a ribbon of packed dirt between the high banks of the dead river. The quiet was thick, broken only by the scuff of Mo’s bare feet and the clink of Wen’s gourd. Mo stopped at a wide, flat patch of mud, smoothed by years of foot traffic, and sat down with a grunt that seemed to come from her very bones.

"Let us do the arithmetic properly," Mo said. She pulled a small, square board from her jacket pocket. It was made of thin wood, covered in chalk marks and grease stains. She wiped a clean space with her sleeve. "This boat. It is two meters long, one meter wide. How deep does it sit when full?"

"The fifth hand," Wen recited, still standing.

"Good. Five hands is roughly twenty centimeters. The volume of water displaced is the length times the width times the depth. Do the math."

Wen sat on the hard ground, her legs folding beneath her. She looked at the board. "Two by one by zero point two," she murmured. "That is zero point two cubic meters."

"And one cubic meter of water," Mo said, leaning forward, "weighs one thousand kilograms. So the boat, when floating, displaces two hundred kilograms of water. But the boat itself weighs more than that, because it is made of wood, which is denser than water, and it carries iron fittings, and rope, and the memory of all the cargo it has carried."

Wen did the multiplication in her head, her fingers twitching on her knee. "If the boat is half wood, half air, and the wood is heavy..." She stopped. Her face went pale, the color draining out of her cheeks like water from a basin. "The boat weighs more than two hundred kilograms. It must weigh three hundred. Maybe four."

"Four hundred kilograms," Mo said, her voice soft and terrifyingly accurate. "That is four hundred kilograms of wood and iron that you would have to lift, with your hands, out of the mud, to get it to float. And you would have to hold it there while you dug the trench, and then let it go, and hope it does not sink again. Do you feel the burden of it yet?"

Wen looked at her hands. They were trembling, a fine, persistent vibration that started in her fingertips and climbed up her wrists. She thought of the cold that had rushed through her arms at the pool, the way her breath had fogged in the morning air. She had not realized the scale of the debt. It was not a small, manageable thing. It was a mountain.
pages.image: Wen sitting on dry mud, face pale, hands trembling, Auntie Mo holding a chalk-marked board, empty river banks in background, harsh sunlight.

pages.text:
Mo did not let her sit in the fear. She stood, brushed the dust from her grey trousers, and pointed to a spot ten meters ahead. The mud there was drier, and the bank sloped gently into the dead channel.

"Watch," she said.

Mo drove the spade into the earth with a sharp, decisive thrust. She did not dig deep. She dug wide. Scooping the mud out, she tossed it to the side, not in a pile, but in a low, long ridge running parallel to the trench. Her work had a rhythm, almost musical; the spade bit the soil with a low note, the mud landing in a soft, continuous strip.

"Dig the channel deep," Mo said, not looking up. "Keep the levee low. If the levee is high, the water hits it and breaks. If the levee is low, the water slides over it and stays with you. You are not building a wall. You are building a guide."

Wen watched the shape emerging from the flat ground. It was a simple, elegant line, a groove in the earth that seemed to invite the water to follow. It was the kind of engineering that did not need to be explained, only seen. Practical, unglamorous, and completely effective.

She picked up the spade. It was heavier than it looked, the weight distributed awkwardly in her hand. She drove it into the mud, and the ground resisted, gritty and stubborn. She leaned into it, her shoulders aching, her breath coming in short, sharp bursts. The mud came up in clumps, dark and rich, smelling of damp earth and old rain.

She threw it into the low ridge Mo had started. The ridge grew, inch by inch, a slow, deliberate line of earth running alongside the trench. Wen’s arms burned, a deep, dull heat that spread from her shoulders to her elbows. She did not stop. She could not stop. The rhythm was there, the same rhythm as her breathing, the same rhythm as the river, if the river had ever had one.

Mo checked the slope of the levee, running her hand along the top. "Good," she said. "Keep it smooth. No bumps. Water hates bumps. Bumps are where it gets stuck."

Wen smoothed the ridge with her palms, pressing the mud flat and firm. It was a small, tactile act, a conversation with the ground. She could feel the moisture in the soil, the coolness of it, the life that lay dormant beneath the surface. It was not magic. It was work. And for the first time, the work felt like a language she was learning to speak.
pages.image: Wen digging a shallow trench, piling mud into a low levee, spade in hand, sweat on her brow, dry river bed, late morning light.

pages.text:
As the sun climbed higher, the heat pressed down on the dry channel, shrinking the world to the dusty patch of ground where they worked. Yet they were not alone. A thin trail of boats had gathered on the mud bar, a ragged line of stranded vessels stretching back into the mist.

A salt-trader, heavyset in a white robe, sat on his bench with a cup of cold tea. He grumbled about the price of salt and the river having been "tapped" upstream, his voice a low, continuous rumble of complaint. Beside him, a family huddled in the shade with a flock of ducks. The birds were quiet and dusty, their feathers matted with silt. A monk with a small brass bell sat cross-legged on the ground, eyes closed, lips moving in silent prayer directed at the mud rather than the sky.

They did not speak to Wen, but they watched her. The salt-trader’s eyes were sharp, calculating her strength and resolve. The family’s children pointed at her, fingers small and accusing, treating her presence as both hope and threat. When the monk finally struck his bell, the note rang out clear and pure in the dry air, a sound that seemed to belong to a cleaner world.

Wen paused, her spade resting in the mud. She looked at the boats, the people, the long silent line of stranded lives. They were not just waiting for water. They were waiting for a reason to keep going. And she, with her trembling hands and aching shoulders, was the only one who held the power to give them that reason.

Mo worked beside her, the spade moving in steady, efficient rhythm. She did not look up, but her voice was low, just loud enough for Wen to hear. "They are counting on you," Mo said. "That is a heavy thing to carry. Heavier than the boat."

Wen looked at her hands. The tremor was still there, a faint, persistent vibration. But beneath it lay a steadiness, a quiet determination growing in her chest since morning. She was not just carrying the boat. She was carrying the hope of a dozen people, the burden of their lives, their futures, their faith in a girl who could move water.

It was a terrifying thought. And a beautiful one.
pages.image: A line of stranded boats on a mudbar, a salt-trader in white, a family with ducks, a monk with a bell, Wen and Mo working in the foreground, dusty atmosphere.

pages.text:
Twilight settled over the dry channel, turning the sky a bruised purple as the air cooled into stillness. The trench they had dug lay finished, a long, smooth groove cutting through the mud from the edge of the remaining pool to the stern of the ferry. A low levee ran alongside it, a gentle ridge that guided the eye and the water along its path with the same patience used to steer a boat through rapids.

Wen stood at the pool’s edge, her hands outstretched, fingers trembling against the cooling air. The water itself was low, a thin, shimmering ribbon that barely covered the basin’s bottom. It was not much, certainly not enough to float a heavy hull, but it was enough to start.

She closed her eyes. Lifting felt wrong, a brute force that would shatter the delicate balance. Instead, she thought of the trench, the levee, the path. She thought of water’s desire to flow, to find the lowest road, to return to the sea. She did not pull. She invited.

The water moved. It did not rise in a sphere, nor did it spiral into the air. It flowed, a thin, silver ribbon lifting from the pool and sliding into the trench, following the line of the levee with a precision that felt almost eerie. It moved slowly, deliberately, a stream of light weaving through the dust and dry earth.

The ferry shuddered. The wood creaked, a deep, resonant sound that vibrated in Wen’s bones. The boat lifted, inch by inch, until the hull was clear of the mud, floating on that thin, shimmering ribbon.

The crowd on the mud bar erupted. The salt-trader stood, his cup of cold tea forgotten in his hand. The family’s children screamed, their voices high and bright against the twilight. The monk struck his bell, a single, clear note that rang out over the silence, a sound of triumph and relief.

Wen stood still, her hands outstretched, the water flowing through her like a cool, steady current connecting her to the earth and the people. She looked down at her fingertips. The white frost was there, a thin, delicate bloom spreading from her nails to her knuckles. It was cold, a biting, persistent chill that did not fade with the movement of the water.

Mo stood beside her, watching the boat float, watching the crowd cheer. Her eyes were on Wen’s hands, sharp and knowing. She said nothing. She did not need to. The silence was a language of its own, a warning, a promise, a debt that had been paid and would be paid again.

The river was moving. And the cost was beginning to show.
